t: Shortest Subarray With OR at Least K I — Brute Force and Sliding Window
o: We need the shortest contiguous subarray whose bitwise OR is at least $k$. Since OR only accumulates bits, extending a subarray can never decrease its OR value. In Example 1, [3] alone has OR 3 ≥ 2, so answer is 1. In Example 2, no single element or pair reaches 10; [2,1,8] gives 11, so answer is 3. In Example 3, k = 0 means any non-empty subarray works (OR of non-negative numbers is ≥ 0), so answer is 1. With n ≤ 50 and values ≤ 50 (< 6 bits), even an O(n²) brute force is trivially fast, but a sliding window achieves O(n · B) where B is the bit count.
k: OR is monotone under extension: adding elements to a subarray never lowers its OR value.
Because values are < 64, each number has at most 6 bits, so we can maintain per-bit counts in O(1) space.
A shrinking sliding window works: expand right while OR < k, shrink left while the window stays special.
If k = 0, any single element qualifies immediately.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over All Subarrays
a.i: Check every subarray (i, j): keep a running OR from i to j, and if it reaches k, record j - i + 1 as a candidate answer. Since OR is monotone, once the running OR hits k for a fixed i, longer subarrays starting at i cannot be shorter, but they may still be needed if none earlier qualified — simply track the minimum over all pairs.
s: For each start index i, set cur = 0.
For each end index j ≥ i, update cur |= nums[j].
If cur >= k, set ans = min(ans, j - i + 1) and break (longer windows are worse).
a.t: O(n²) — all pairs (i, j), with an early break when the window becomes special.
a.sp: O(1) — only a running OR value.

a.n: Approach 2: Sliding Window with Per-Bit Counts
a.i: Maintain a window [left, right] and count how many elements inside contribute each of the ~30 bits. The window's OR is computable in O(B). Expand right until OR ≥ k; then shrink left as long as the window remains special, recording lengths. Because OR is monotone, this finds every minimal special window ending at each right index.
s: Keep cnt[bit] = number of window elements having that bit set.
For each right, add nums[right]'s bits to cnt and recompute cur = OR of present bits.
While cur >= k, record ans = min(ans, right - left + 1), remove nums[left]'s bits, increment left, and recompute cur.
After processing all rights, return ans, or -1 if never updated.
a.t: O(n · B) — each element enters and leaves the window once, with B ≈ 6–32 bit updates per operation.

w: In an interview, mention the O(n²) brute force first (it's fully sufficient given n ≤ 50), then offer the sliding window as the scalable solution — especially relevant since the hard version of this problem has much larger constraints. Pitfalls: forgetting k = 0 (any element qualifies, both approaches handle it naturally); not recomputing cur correctly after removing an element — you must clear a bit only when its count drops to zero; and returning -1 when no window ever satisfies the condition. Likely follow-ups: solve the harder version with large n and large values (same sliding-window idea), or handle queries / streaming input.
